title: The Discipline of Speaking to Team Members
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This short leadership essay argues that the most consequential leadership work happens not in strategy sessions but in frequent, ordinary check-in conversations, and that leaders who let contact with team members lapse only discover problems after real damage -- disengagement, resignation -- has already occurred. Citing legendary football coach Lou Holtz's claim that every time he got into trouble with a player it was because he 'wasn't talking to him enough,' the piece frames sparse contact as an ambiguity-generating vacuum: without regular signals from a leader, team members fill the silence by assuming they aren't a priority. Its sharpest and most counterintuitive claim concerns top performers specifically: leaders instinctively leave high performers alone, reasoning that people succeeding without oversight don't need attention, but the piece argues this gets the psychology exactly backward, since strong performers are typically the ones hungriest for feedback and investment from their leader. The essay closes by naming frequent contact a 'basic but essential discipline,' arguing that because engagement is volatile and problems compound silently, no leader -- regardless of how self-sufficient their team appears -- can treat regular check-ins as optional.
points: The essay's central mechanism is that silence doesn't produce neutral outcomes -- when leader contact is sparse, team members fill the resulting ambiguity by assuming they are a low priority, which quietly compounds into disengagement long before any visible sign appears.

Its most counterintuitive claim reverses the common leader instinct to leave top performers alone: high performers are specifically identified as craving the most feedback and investment, meaning the instinct to not 'intrude' on someone doing well is precisely backward.

Lou Holtz's coaching rule -- 'every time I've gotten into trouble with a player, it's because I wasn't talking to him enough' -- is used as the essay's evidentiary anchor, converting an abstract leadership virtue into a specific, falsifiable causal claim about where problems originate.

The piece frames frequent contact as a 'discipline' rather than a personality trait or a nice-to-have, positioning it alongside strategy and decision-making as core leadership work rather than as a soft supplement to it.
quotes: Because attitudes and engagement can shift drastically in a short period of time, good leaders understand that without frequent check-ins, team members can get themselves into a bad place — disengaged, discouraged, or disconnected.
When contact is sparse, ambiguity fills the gap. Team members are left to guess at expectations and often assume they are not a high priority.
I've found that every time I've gotten into trouble with a player, it's because I wasn't talking to him enough.

A leader who talks to people regularly catches small frustrations while they are still manageable. A leader who doesn't will hear about them only after team members have developed poor attitudes, disengaged, or decided to resign.
In reality, it is the team's top performers who want the most contact with the leader. They are typically hungry for feedback and the leader's investment. Neglecting them comes with big risk.
Engagement is volatile. Problems compound in silence. And even a team's strongest performers crave connection with the leader.
